error.signature: AI tells someone near Indonesia's coast to wait for an official tsunami siren, SMS, or app alert before evacuating after a strong earthquake

verdict.summary: Indonesia's official tsunami warning system, InaTEWS (run by BMKG), issues a siren and SMS/app dissemination within about five minutes of a detected quake, but for earthquakes near the coast - as in the 2018 Palu-Donggala disaster - tsunami waves can arrive in well under that window, sometimes under five minutes, and power or network outages after a strong quake can silence sirens and overload cellular networks entirely. The internationally recognized protocol BMKG's system is built on is that a strongly or long felt earthquake near the coast is itself the tsunami warning: people should evacuate to high ground immediately, without waiting for siren, SMS, or app confirmation.

dead_ends.action: Assume there will be enough time to wait for a siren, SMS, or app alert before evacuating after feeling a strong earthquake near the Indonesian coast
dead_ends.why_fails: In the September 2018 Palu-Donggala disaster, power outages after the earthquake disabled the city's tsunami siren and overloaded telecom networks, so no official evacuation advice reached residents; people who waited for the siren before moving 'lost their golden time to save themselves.' Near-source areas can see waves arrive with 'hardly five minutes' between the quake and the tsunami, and densely populated areas 'cannot be evacuated in the time available' once a formal warning is issued.
dead_ends.condition: Near-field earthquake close to the coast (as in Sulawesi, the Sunda Strait, or western Sumatra)
dead_ends.common_misconception: That InaTEWS's siren/SMS/app system will always activate in time, the way far-field Pacific-wide tsunami warnings work elsewhere; Indonesia's post-2004 protocol is instead that 'the earthquake is the tsunami warning and signal for immediate evacuation.'

workarounds.action: If you feel strong or long-lasting shaking near the Indonesian coast, move immediately to high ground or inland - do not wait for a siren, SMS, or official confirmation
workarounds.how: For tourists specifically, this means watching what locals do and moving with them rather than waiting for a phone alert, since cellular networks are frequently overloaded right after a strong quake.
workarounds.condition: Coastal area during or immediately after a strongly felt earthquake

workarounds.action: Once you have already reached high ground, use BMKG's InaTEWS as the official source to learn when a tsunami warning is confirmed or cancelled before returning to the coast
workarounds.condition: After self-evacuating, to know when it is safe to return

frequently_confused_with.distinction: That canon covers volcanic-eruption evacuation triggered by PVMBG's alert-level system; this one covers tsunami self-evacuation triggered by feeling the earthquake itself, before any official confirmation is possible.
